newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia's China investment not to change due to Deng.
newsitem.headline: Asia's China investment not to change due to Deng.

text.p: China's efforts to ensure a smooth transition of power before the death of its paramount leader Deng Xiaoping should prevent major shifts in investment strategy by its Asian neighbours, business executives said.
"Deng's death has not changed (our) outlook on China. I don't think the business environment has changed," said Inderbethal Singh Thakral, managing director of Thakral Corp Ltd in Thailand.
Thakral supplies consumer electronic products to China, which accounts for about 85 percent of its business.

"The transfer of power has been pretty smooth and the new team is pretty well established," C.W. Toh, chief financial officer of KFC Holdings (M) Bhd in Malaysia, said of the outlook for China following Deng's death.
However, some executives said that even without Deng's death they were viewing their investments in China cautiously because of the tough business environment.
"Since last year, companies have realised it is tough to make money in China, so large-scale investment is declining," said Takashi Hoshino, an economist at LTCB Research Institute in Tokyo.
Japanese companies are concerned about doing business in China because of the way the Chinese have watered down policies that promoted foreign investment with preferential treatment.

An official at the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) said he expects the pace of Japanese investment in China to slow this year. It had dropped to about $3.06 billion in the first half of 1996 from $7.58 billion in all of 1995, JETRO said.

Tim Meakin, chief excecutive officer of Australian pharmaceutical maker F.H. Faulding & Co Ltd, said he did not expect China to make any changes in its policies toward Western investment following Deng's death.
But he said it had become more difficult doing business there in the past six months because of Beijing's austerity programme.
"The last six months in China have been fairly tough," he said. "We would hope the future will be a little less restrictive."
Still, the commitment to China remains.
A prominent Taiwan business leader said he did not expect the island's investment in China to change.
"Taiwan investments (in China) will not change," said Kao Ching-yuan, chief executive officer of Taiwan's top China investor President Enterprises.
Some 30,000 Taiwan-funded businesses have invested an estimated US$20 billion in China since Taipei began allowing indirect contact with the mainland in the mid-1980s.

Deng has been hailed for ushering in a new era of economic and financial reforms designed to bring prosperity to the country by replacing its strict economic planning with a more pragmatic, free-market style, approach.
Rumours he was near death had surfaced frequently in recent years. The most recent round began just last week and caused a shakeout in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan stock markets.

"I don't think it's going to have much of an impact with the successor in place. We're not going to react to it whatsoever (in changing our investment strategy)," Robert Coombe, executive director of Commerce Asset Fund Managers in Malaysia said.
"Really, the market has been expecting the news for some time," he added.
